newsitem.title: USA: Exasperated analysts may seek muni bond boycott.
newsitem.headline: Exasperated analysts may seek muni bond boycott.

text.p: Bond analysts, fed up with the cold shoulder they get from some issuers when they seek financial updates, may urge major buyers soon to boycott the issuers' bonds, a spokesman said Monday.
Jeffrey Baker, head of the National Federation of Municipal Analysts (NFMA), said the group will release a "position paper" on the issue by Labor Day.

The paper will express analysts' exasperation with the barebones compliance by some localities with Securities and Exchange Commission's muni disclosure Rule 15c2-12, Baker said in a telephone interview.

Adopted in November 1994, Rule 15c2-12 bars dealers from underwriting bond offerings unless issuers pledge to provide annual financial information and notices of 11 specific "material events" to the market.
Issuers supply the data, at minimum, by sending it to nationally recognized municipal securities information repositories (NRMSIRs).

Baker said analysts are frustrated with bond lawyers who are telling clients to keep disclosure to the minimum 11 events spelled out in SEC's rule. Examples are principal and interest payment delinquencies, unscheduled draws on debt service, and others.
Some lawyers also tell clients to stop forwarding information directly to analysts, Baker said. Instead, analysts must pay fees to get the data from repositories, Baker said.

"We find it almost an afront," Baker said. "Directors of finance have been told to take this position by their counsel. They, themselves, didn't wake up some morning and decide not to do it," he said.
Baker said analysts will highlight the problem before summer's end. "We want to nip this in the bud now before more people take that position," he said.

Baker said the group will make the position paper available to regulators, market participants, and the press. No final decision has been made, but the paper may urge buyers to boycott the bonds of uncooperative issuers, he said.
The paper will be NFMA's second stab at the problem this year.

Analysts met with SEC's Office of Municipal Securities on May 20 on the issue and was expected to hand over names of some problem issuers. The group says hospitals and below investment grade issuers are the biggest culprits.
